survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The Survey of Adult Skills 2023 country notes report results for Germany using a household survey design with a personal interview and a self-completed digital assessment administered on tablets. The sample (4793 adults aged 16–65) was drawn to be representative of about 53.2 million adults aged 16–65 residing in Germany at the time of data collection, and the OECD reports that analyses were conducted to check that non-response does not introduce significant bias. The excerpt does not name specific sampling or replicate weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT or BRR/jackknife), so the exact weight variable(s) used in the underlying OECD analyses cannot be confirmed from the provided text. For analysts using the microdata, the appropriate approach is to apply the official Survey of Adult Skills sampling weights and replicate weights (if provided in the dataset) to obtain correct standard errors and confidence intervals for mean scores and proficiency-level shares.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses are based on adults aged 16–65 in Germany who participated in the Survey of Adult Skills 2022–23. The note states that the sample was drawn to be representative of about 53.2 million adults aged 16–65 residing in Germany, and that non-response bias checks were conducted. For comparability across cycles, the note indicates that doorstep-only respondents (administered only the doorstep interview due to a language barrier) are generally excluded when comparing results across cycles; the note also states that some outcome figures exclude doorstep-only respondents. No further analytic exclusions (e.g., item nonresponse thresholds) are specified in the excerpt.

data.outcome_summary: The OECD Survey of Adult Skills 2023 country note for Germany reports adult proficiency in three domains—literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem solving—assessed in 2022–23 among adults aged 16–65. Germany participated for the second time (first participation in 2011–12), enabling trend comparisons. The assessment is exclusively administered on digital devices (tablets) and proficiency is reported on 500-point scales with proficiency levels derived from task success/failure; uncertainty is shown via 95% confidence intervals. The note reports mean scores and the distribution across proficiency levels (e.g., shares at Level 1 or below and at Levels 4–5), and it also summarizes relationships between skills and outcomes such as employment, wages, life satisfaction, health, political efficacy, trust, volunteering, and job–skills mismatch. For some comparisons, respondents who were only administered the doorstep interview due to language barriers are excluded to maximize comparability across cycles.
